'''Friedwardt Winterberg''' (born June 12, 1929) is a German-American [[theoretical physicist]] and was a [[research professor]] at the [[University of Nevada, Reno]]. He is known for his research in areas spanning [[general relativity]], [[Planck units|Planck scale physics]], [[nuclear fusion]], and [[Plasma (physics)|plasmas]]. His work in [[nuclear physics|nuclear]] [[Spacecraft propulsion|rocket propulsion]] earned him the 1979 [[Hermann Oberth]] Gold Medal of the [[Wernher von Braun]] International Space Flight Foundation<ref>Astronautics & Aeronautics Magazine, AIAA, v. 17, p 83, 1979, {{ISSN|0004-6213}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1063/1.2995324 | title = Winterberg is Hermann Oberth Gold Medalist | journal = [[Physics Today]] | volume = 32 | issue = 12 | pages = 64 | date=December 1979 }}</ref><ref name="faculty bio">[http://www.physics.unr.edu/FacWinterberg.html Bio] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080423120226/http://physics.unr.edu/FacWinterberg.html |date=2008-04-23 }} from the [[University of Nevada, Reno]] website.</ref> and a 1981 citation by the Nevada Legislature.<ref name="faculty bio"/><ref>Nevada Legislature, Statutes of the State of Nevada passed at the 61st Session of the Legislature, Senate Concurrent Resolution no. 68, William S. Hein & Co, 1981</ref> He is also an honorary member of the German Aerospace Society Lilienthal-Oberth.

His only child is Astrid Winterberg.{{cn|reason=an unregistered user added this information and we have no way to verify it.|date=May 2024}}

==Background==
Winterberg was born in 1929 in [[Berlin, Germany]]. In 1953 he received his MSc from the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|University of Frankfurt]] working under [[Friedrich Hund]], and in 1955 he received his PhD in physics from the [[Max Planck Institute]], [[Göttingen]], as a student of [[Werner Heisenberg]]. In 1959, Winterberg emigrated to the United States as part of [[Operation Paperclip]].<ref name=Hunt>{{cite book |last=Hunt|first=Linda|title=''Secret Agenda: The United States Government, Nazi Scientists, and Project Paperclip, 1945 to 1990''|year=1991|publisher=St.Martin's Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-312-05510-3|pages=6,21,31,176,204,259}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B7RV_vASz0EC&pg=PR7 | title=The Release of Thermonuclear Energy by Inertial Confinement: Ways Towards Ignition| isbn=9789814295918| last1=Winterberg| first1=Friedwardt| year=2010| publisher=World Scientific}}</ref> Friedwardt was 15 at the end of the war. Paperclip continued to recruit German scientists through the [[Cold War]] to prevent them from working for the Soviets.

==Work==
Winterberg is known for his work in the fields of [[nuclear fusion]] and [[plasma physics]], and [[Edward Teller]] has been quoted as saying that he had "perhaps not received the attention he deserves" for his work on fusion.<ref name="king 171">{{harvnb|King|1989|p=171}}</ref> He is an elected member of the Paris-based [[International Academy of Astronautics]], in which he sat on the Committee of Interstellar Space Exploration.<ref name="regents minutes">Cited in the University of Nevada System Board of Regents' Meeting Minutes, April 12–13, 1990. Online at [http://system.nevada.edu/Board-of-R/Meetings/Minutes/1990/1990/19900412.htm_cvt.htm Nevada.edu] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902024603/http://system.nevada.edu/Board-of-R/Meetings/Minutes/1990/1990/19900412.htm_cvt.htm |date=2006-09-02 }} Retrieved February 17, 2006.</ref> According to his faculty webpage, in 1954 he "made the first proposal to test [[general relativity]] with [[atomic clock]]s in earth satellites" and his thermonuclear microexplosion ignition concept<ref>F. Winterberg, "Rocket propulsion by thermonuclear microbombs ignited with intense relativistic electron beams", Raumfahrtforschung 15, 208-217 (1971).</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Matloff|2005|p=80}}</ref> was adopted by the [[British Interplanetary Society]] for their [[Project Daedalus]] Starship Study.<ref name="faculty bio"/><ref>Alan Bond and Anthony R. Martin, [[Project Daedalus]] - Final Report, Journal of The British Interplanetary Society, pp. S1-S192, 1978.</ref>

His research in the 21st century has been on the "Planck Aether Hypothesis", a theory that claims to "explain both [[quantum mechanics]] and the [[theory of relativity]] as [[asymptote|asymptotic]] low energy approximations, and gives a spectrum of particles greatly resembling the [[Standard Model|standard model]]. [[Einstein field equations|Einstein's gravitational]] and [[Maxwell's equations|Maxwell's electromagnetic equations]] are unified by the symmetric and antisymmetric wave mode of a vortex sponge, [[Dirac spinor]]s result from gravitationally interacting bound positive-negative mass vortices, which explains why the mass of an electron is so much smaller than the [[Planck mass]]."<ref>Winterberg (2002).</ref> The theory proposes that the only free parameters in the fundamental equations of physics are the [[Planck length]], [[Planck mass|mass]], and [[Planck time|time]], and shows why [[Euclidean space|<math>\R^3</math>]] is the natural space, as [[Special unitary group|<math>\operatorname{SU}(2)</math>]] is treated as the fundamental [[Group (mathematics)|group]] [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to [[Special unitary group|<math>\operatorname{SO}(3)</math>]] &mdash; an alternative to [[string field theory|string field theories]] in <math>\R^{10}</math> and [[M theory]] in <math>\R^{11}</math>. It permits the value of the [[fine-structure constant]] at the Planck length to be computed, and this value remarkably agrees with the empirical value.

== Proposal for direct test of general relativity ==
In a 1955 paper Winterberg proposed a test of [[general relativity]] using accurate atomic clocks placed in orbit in artificial satellites.<ref>Winterberg, Relativistische Zeitdilatation eines künstlichen Satelliten, Astronautica Acta, Vol. 2, no. 1, pp. 25-29 1956</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bourabai.kz/winter/satelliten.htm |title=Bourabai.kz |access-date=2009-06-26 |archive-date=2014-07-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140703080406/http://bourabai.kz/winter/satelliten.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>  At that time atomic clocks were not yet of the required accuracy and artificial satellites did not exist. [[Werner Heisenberg]] wrote a letter to Winterberg in 1957 in which he said the idea sounded "very interesting".<ref>{{harvnb|Winterberg|2002|p=262}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://bourabai.narod.ru/winter/img/heizen-letter.gif | format = GIF | title = Letter from Werner Heisenberg | publisher = Narod.ru }}</ref>

== Fusion activism ==
[[File:Winterberg Daedalus Reaction Chamber.jpg|thumb|300px|Courtesy NASA Marshall Space Flight Center and University of Alabama in Huntsville]]

Winterberg has published numerous articles in the area of [[inertial confinement fusion]]. In particular, Winterberg is known for the idea of [[Macron (physics)|impact fusion]] and the concept of the magnetically insulated diode for the generation of multi-megampere megavolt ion beams for the purpose of heating plasmas to thermonuclear fusion temperatures. He conceived of a nuclear fusion propulsion reactor for space travel, which is called the Winterberg / Daedalus Class<ref>M. W. Turner, C. W. Hawk, R. J. Litchford, Experiments in Magnetic Flux Compression using Plasma Armatures, 12th Annual NASA/JPL/MSFC Advanced Space Propulsion Workshop</ref> Magnetic Compression Reaction Chamber, which was later developed at the University of Alabama at Huntsville's Propulsion Research Center.  Most recently he has designed a giant spacecraft, propelled with [[deuterium]] micro-detonations ignited by a GeV proton beam, drawn from the spacecraft acting as an electrically charged up and magnetically insulated capacitor.<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=0812.0397 |title=Deuterium microbomb rocket propulsion |date=December 2, 2008| last1 = Winterberg | first1 = Friedwardt | author-link = Friedwardt Winterberg |bibcode = 2008arXiv0812.0397W }}</ref> Winterberg also developed ideas for mining increasingly rare industrially crucial elements on planetary bodies such as the moon using fusion detonation devices. He became involved with the idea of using beam weapons in outer space in the late 1970s while working at the [[Desert Research Institute]].

According to Dennis King, Winterberg shared his ideas on beam weapons with the U.S. Air Force and he speculated on the subject in publications for the [[Fusion Energy Foundation]] (FEF), a part of the [[Lyndon LaRouche]] [[LaRouche movement|movement]]. The FEF published a book of Winterberg describing the design [[Teller-Ulam design|of the hydrogen bomb]], with the hope of getting research in inertial confinement fusion declassified. Winterberg also contributed articles and interviews to the FEF magazine, ''Fusion'', and its successor magazine, ''[[21st Century Science and Technology]]''. He also participated in a 1985 conference jointly sponsored by the FEF and the [[Schiller Institute]], speaking on the topic of [[X-ray laser]]s, the [[Strategic Defense Initiative]] and [[interstellar travel]].<ref name="colonize1985">Colonize Space, New Benjamin Franklin House, New York, N.Y. 1985</ref>  The conference attracted a number of scientists interested in promoting fusion scientific research;<ref name="colonize1985"/> Winterberg was never a member of any of LaRouche's political organisations.

On November 12, 2007, Winterberg addressed the [[American Physical Society]] Plasma Physics Convention in Orlando, Florida, encouraging efforts to achieve economically feasible fusion energy, and presenting his ideas for what direction the efforts should take. Winterberg stresses inertial confinement fusion.

Back in 1963, it was proposed by Winterberg<ref>F. Winterberg, ''[[Z. Naturforsch. A]]'', '''19''', 231 (1964)</ref> that the ignition of thermonuclear micro-explosions, could be achieved by an intense beam of [[macron (physics)|microparticles]] accelerated to a velocity of 1000&nbsp;km/s. And in 1968,<ref>F. Winterberg, Phys. Rev. 174, 212 (1968)</ref>  Winterberg proposed to use intense electron and ion beams, generated by Marx generators, for the same purpose. Most recently, Winterberg has proposed the ignition of a deuterium microexplosion, with a gigavolt super-Marx generator, which is a [[Marx generator|Marx Generator]] driven by up to 100 ordinary Marx generators.<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv = 0812.0394 | last1 = Winterberg | first1 = Friedwardt | author-link = Friedwardt Winterberg | title = Ignition of a deuterium micro-detonation with a gigavolt super marx generator | date = December 1, 2008 |bibcode = 2009JFuE...28..290W | doi=10.1007/s10894-008-9189-3 | volume=28 | issue = 3 | journal=Journal of Fusion Energy | pages=290–295| s2cid = 15286588 }}</ref>

== Rudolph controversy ==
In 1983, Winterberg became involved in disputes concerning the engineer [[Arthur Rudolph]], who had been brought to the United States after [[World War II]] as part of [[Operation Paperclip]] to work on the U.S. rocketry program.  It was Rudolph who then designed the [[Saturn V]] rocket that launched [[Neil Armstrong]] to the Moon. In the early 1980s, Rudolph's record as a potential [[Nazi war criminal]] at [[Mittelwerk]] surfaced and became the center of a political controversy after the [[Office of Special Investigations (United States Department of Justice)|Office of Special Investigations]] (OSI) negotiated to have him renounce his U.S. citizenship, purportedly under duress,<ref name="Franklin, 141">{{harvnb|Franklin|1987|p=141}}</ref> after which he returned to Germany.  After a thorough investigation by German authorities, it was decided there was no basis for prosecution and his German citizenship was restored. Rudolph pursued lawsuits hoping to regain his US citizenship but was barred entry to the US in 1989.{{citation needed|date=February 2019}}

Winterberg lobbied in favour of Rudolph,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://lyndonlarouchewatch.org/fascism10.htm |title=Chapter 10, Lyndon LaRouche and the New American Fascism |publisher=Lyndonlarouchewatch.org |date=1987-09-03 |access-date=2009-06-24}}</ref> giving interviews to magazines, launching his own separate investigation, and speaking in Rudolph's defense at a conference hosted by [[Lyndon LaRouche]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://articles.philly.com/1986-03-07/news/26083229_1_mittelwerk-rudolph-case-arthur-rudolph | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120125071312/http://articles.philly.com/1986-03-07/news/26083229_1_mittelwerk-rudolph-case-arthur-rudolph | url-status=dead | archive-date=January 25, 2012 |title = Archives}}</ref> After the fall of the Berlin wall legal assistant requests by the US Office of Special Investigation to the Communist East German Government regarding the Rudolph case emerged and became part of the public record.<ref> {{ cite web | title = FBI Records: The Vault &mdash; Arthur Rudolph Part 1 of 1 | url = https://vault.fbi.gov/Arthur%20Rudolph%20/Arthur%20Rudolph%20Part%201%20of%201 }} </ref>

== Einstein–Hilbert dispute ==
{{main|General relativity priority dispute}}
Winterberg was also involved in a dispute relating to the [[history of general relativity]] in a controversy over the publication of the general relativity field equations (both [[Albert Einstein]] and [[David Hilbert]] had each published them within a very short time span). In 1997, [[Leo Corry]], [[Jürgen Renn]], and [[John Stachel]] published an article in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' entitled "Belated decision in the Hilbert-Einstein priority dispute", arguing that, after looking at the original proofs of the article by Hilbert, that they indicated that Hilbert had not anticipated Einstein's equations.<ref>{{harvnb|Corry|Renn|Stachel|1997}}</ref>

Winterberg published a refutation of these conclusions in 2004, observing that the galley proofs of Hilbert's articles had been tampered with &mdash; part of one page had been cut off. He argued that the removed part of the article contained the equations that Einstein later published and alleged that it was part of a "crude attempt by some unknown individual to falsify the historical record." He alleged that ''Science'' had refused to print the article and thus he was forced to publish it in ''[[Zeitschrift für Naturforschung]]''.  Winterberg's article argued that despite the missing part of the proofs, that the correct crucial Field Equation is still imbedded on other pages of the proofs, in various forms, including Hilbert's variational principle with correct Lagrangian from which the Field Equation is immediately derived.<ref>Winterberg (2004).</ref> Winterberg presented his findings at the American Physical Society meeting in Tampa, Florida in April 2005.{{Citation needed|date=April 2009}}

Corry, Renn, and Stachel authored a joint reply to Winterberg, which they claimed ''Zeitschrift für Naturforschung'' refused to publish without "unacceptable" modifications, and unable to find a publisher elsewhere, they made it available on the internet. The reply accused Winterberg of misrepresenting the reason why ''Science'' would not publish his paper (it had to do with the section of the journal it was scheduled to appear in), and also misrepresenting that the paper published in ''Zeitschrift für Naturforschung'' was the same paper he had submitted to ''Science'', and had in fact been "substantially altered" after Winterberg had received their comments on an earlier draft. Actually, Winterberg in his Final Comment had clearly stated that the paper submitted to Science had been a ''previous version''. They then argue that Winterberg's interpretation of the Hilbert paper was incorrect, that the lost part of the page was unlikely to have been consequential, and that much of Winterberg's reasoning about what could be in the missing piece was incorrect (down to noting Winterberg claims that 1/3 of the page was removed, when actually over half a page is missing total from the two cut off pages) and internally inconsistent. They further argued there was a likely "non-paranoid" explanation for the missing part of the page.<ref>{{harvnb|Corry|Renn|Stachel|2004}}</ref>

Later, the original reply to Winterberg was removed from their website and replaced with a much shorter statement saying only that Winterberg's conclusions were incorrect, specifically that he had focused on the missing page fragment, "a fact without any bearing on the matter at hand", while failing "to address the substantive difference between the theory expounded in the proofs" of Hilbert. The statement further said that Winterberg had apparently indicated that he was "personally offended" by the original response, the "Max Planck Institute for the History of Science has decided to replace the original, more detailed response to his paper with this abbreviated version".<ref>{{harvnb|Corry|Renn|Stachel|2005}}</ref> This was, apparently, because the original reply had contained two very derisive statements against Professor Winterberg; later, the Max Planck Society released a note distancing itself from those two statements, without commenting on the underlying scientific dispute.<ref>[http://www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/texts/Winterberg-Antwort.html untitled note], Max Planck Society, 14 September 2005</ref>
